title: Printing Variables and Template Literals
summary: Combine labels and variables in output using commas, the + operator, and template literals.
intro: Real output mixes fixed text with values from your variables. JavaScript gives you three ways to do it: pass several arguments to `console.log`, join strings with `+`, or write a template literal. You will use template literals for almost everything after this lesson.

steps.title: Variables in console.log
steps.body:
Pass a label and a variable to `console.log` with a comma between them. It prints each argument in order with one space between, so you never type that space yourself.

```javascript
const score = 90;
console.log("Score:", score); // Score: 90
```

You can mix as many labels and variables as you like in one call. Text goes in quotes, variables do not.

```javascript
const player = "Mia";
const level = 4;
console.log(player, "reached level", level); // Mia reached level 4
```

Watch the spaces. Because `console.log` adds one between every argument, writing `"Score: ", score` prints two spaces after the colon. Leave the trailing space out of the label.

example.title: Profile lines
example.prompt: Print three lines about a person using comma-separated arguments.
example.output:
Name: Ada
Age: 36
Ada lives in London
example.explanation: Each call prints its arguments left to right with a single space between them. The number `36` prints as is, and the third call mixes two variables with a label in the middle.

practice.title: Product lines
practice.prompt:
Print three lines about a product using comma-separated arguments.

1. Print the label `Item:` and the variable `item`.
2. Print the label `Price:` and the variable `price`.
3. Print `item`, the text `comes in`, and `color` in one call.

Expected output:

```text
Item: Lamp
Price: 25
Lamp comes in blue
```

tests.output:
Item: Lamp
Price: 25
Lamp comes in blue

hints: Each line is one `console.log` call with its pieces separated by commas.
Leave the space off the end of `"Item:"`. `console.log` already adds one between arguments.
On the last line only `"comes in"` needs quotes. `item` and `color` are variables.

steps.title: Joining strings with +
steps.body:
The `+` operator joins two strings into one. This is called concatenation. Unlike commas in `console.log`, `+` adds nothing between the pieces, so you write every space and punctuation mark yourself.

```javascript
const first = "Grace";
console.log("Hi, " + first + "!"); // Hi, Grace!
```

When one side of `+` is a string, the other side is turned into text. That is the big gotcha: a number stored as text gets glued on, not added.

```javascript
console.log("5" + 3);           // 53
console.log(5 + 3);             // 8
console.log("Total: " + 5 + 3); // Total: 53
```

The last line runs left to right: `"Total: " + 5` is already a string, so `3` is glued on too.

To grow a string step by step, declare it with `let` and use `+=`, which appends to the end.

```javascript
let line = "Ready";
line += ", set";
line += ", go!";
console.log(line); // Ready, set, go!
```

example.title: Greeting message
example.prompt: Build a greeting with + and +=, then show how + treats a string and a number.
example.output:
Hello, Ada! You have 3 new messages.
53
8
example.explanation: The message starts as `"Hello, Ada!"`, and `+=` appends the rest, turning `count` into the text `3`. Notice the space at the start of `" You have "`: `+` never adds one for you. Then `"5" + 3` joins text to make `53`, while `5 + 3` adds two numbers to make `8`.

practice.title: Order summary
practice.prompt:
Build an order summary with + and +=, then compare a string plus a number with a number plus a number.

1. Start `message` as `"Order #" + orderId`.
2. Use `+=` to append `" for "` and `customer`.
3. Use `+=` to append `": "`, `itemCount`, and `" items"`, then print `message`.
4. Print `"10" + 5`, then print `10 + 5`.

Expected output:

```text
Order #42 for Linus: 2 items
105
15
```
hints: Every space and colon must be inside your quotes, for example `" for "`.
Each `+=` line appends a quoted piece and then a variable, joined with `+`.
Quote `"10"` so it is text, and leave `10` unquoted when you want real addition.

steps.title: Template literals
steps.body:
A template literal is a string written with backticks instead of quotes. Inside it, `${...}` inserts the value of a variable or expression right where you write it. No `+` signs, and the spaces you type are the spaces you get.

```javascript
const user = "Sam";
const points = 12;
console.log(`${user} has ${points} points`); // Sam has 12 points
```

Need a dollar sign in front of a value? Write `$` followed by `${...}`: the first `$` is plain text.

```javascript
const cost = 7;
console.log(`Cost: $${cost}`); // Cost: $7
```

A template literal can also span several lines. Every line break inside the backticks is kept, and so is any indentation, so start the following lines at the left edge.

```javascript
const note = `Line one
Line two`;
```

Gotcha: `${...}` only works inside backticks. In `"Hi ${user}"` it prints literally. From now on, use template literals whenever a string contains values.

example.title: Rent sentence and badge
example.prompt: Print a sentence with one template literal, then a three-line badge from one multi-line template literal.
example.output:
Ada (36) lives in London and pays $900 rent
Name: Ada
Age: 36
City: London
example.explanation: Each `${...}` is replaced by its variable's value. In `$${rent}` the first `$` is ordinary text, so it prints `$900`. The badge keeps both line breaks from inside the backticks, so one `console.log` prints three lines.

practice.title: Lamp card
practice.prompt:
Print a product sentence with one template literal, then a three-line product card from one multi-line template literal.

1. Print `Lamp costs $25 and comes in blue` with one template literal that inserts `item`, `price`, and `color`.
2. Set `card` to one template literal with the lines `Item: ...`, `Price: $...`, and `Color: ...`.
3. Print `card`.

Expected output:

```text
Lamp costs $25 and comes in blue
Item: Lamp
Price: $25
Color: blue
```

tests.output:
Lamp costs $25 and comes in blue
Item: Lamp
Price: $25
Color: blue

hints: Use backticks, not quotes, so `${...}` works.
Write `$${price}` to print a dollar sign before the price.
Press Enter inside the backticks to start the next line of the card, and do not indent it.

recap:
- `console.log("Label:", value)` prints the arguments with one space between each.
- `+` joins strings with nothing in between, so you add spaces and punctuation yourself.
- A string plus a number gives text: `"5" + 3` is `53`, but `5 + 3` is `8`.
- `message += "more"` appends to a string stored in a `let`.
- Template literals use backticks and `${...}` to insert values.
- Write `$${price}` for a dollar sign before a value.
- A template literal can span several lines and keeps every line break.
